pitch_detail.notes: A few steps of dirty fifth-class ledges bending leftward lead to a big sloping ledge, then up and right to a clean white finger crack in a right-facing corner. Lieback it for about ten metres to a bolted belay on the face above.
Easier ground with a handful of bolts leads into a right-facing flare. Stem up it and pull the roof, which is the first hard spot. A clean splitter above holds a second hard section before the belay.
Follow an offset splitter crack straight up. Near the top it slants out left to reach the stance and anchor.
Ledges and easy cracks lead up to a clean vertical wall split by the Joint cracks, where this line crosses Shield of Dreams.
A cutter crack that leans to the right on a flat, clean wall.

Begin on the slab left of the belay and traverse right over easier ground to a large white flake that cuts back left about three metres into a short steep left-facing corner. This leads to a crack; stay left of the big triangular roof recess rather than heading up and right into it. Follow the crack for roughly ten metres to a bolted face above, where the hard climbing sits.

review.changed: Wrote all 6 pitches with grades and lengths. Left out the rappel table: text only says all belays are bolted and a 70 m rope works, no station list.
review.other_findings: Text lengths sum to 160 m against stored length_m 213 (likely route length includes approach ledges or a different basis).

pitch_detail.notes: Start under the longest splitter in the middle of the face. Three bolts on thin green rock right off the ground hold the hardest moves. Then an easy broken crack takes medium and small cams, one more bolt where it fades, and a cut left to a large flat belay ledge.

This is the Root Crack. Two bolts get you into the splitter, then it continues for about 40 m with the hardest part inside the first 20 m. Small to medium cams and small to medium stoppers; belay on a ledge out to the right.

Continue up the same splitter to a roof, clip a couple of bolts, and traverse right into a white finger-crack corner. Go up to the next roof, exit left, and finish on the overhanging face with good holds past two last bolts. Bring doubles from the smallest cams to green Camelot, triples in finger sizes, one gold Camelot and shoulder slings.
Short pitch. Hand crack straight up from the belay for about ten metres, then loose blocky ledges for about as far again to the next stance. Medium cams.
Pink face climbing aimed at a roof that slants rightward. Pull over it on its right side, then work back up left to the belay ledge. Five bolts.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches. No rappel table: descent text gives rope length and one intermediate anchor but not a full station list.
review.other_findings: none

pitch_detail.notes: Climb a grey left-facing corner for about eight metres, then step into a perfect finger-width splitter that continues for roughly thirty metres more.

Named for a long streak of quartz beside the cracks. Head right over a few bolts to two body-width cracks, using small cams in the right-hand one, up to a bolt at the hard move. Easier splitters then reach a belay at the top of the quartz.

Straight up from the belay with good stances and good gear. A tricky hard section is protected by small brass nuts and tiny cams. At a large bucket ledge, sling gear and traverse left, then easy ground leads about twelve metres to the belay.

First shift the belay about fifteen metres across second-class ledges to bolts under the Joint crack, where this route crosses Puff the Magic Dragon. A thin crack then goes up and left to a powerful finish on sloping granite holds. Small nuts and tiny cams do the work.
Bolts lead directly above the belay into a long brown dihedral facing right. To reach the summit, go left while still roped to easier ground, then return to the bolts to descend.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches; the belay-shift between P3 and P4 is folded into P4's notes. No rappel table (text only says belays are bolted for a 70 m rope).
review.other_findings: none

pitch_detail.notes: Scalloped cracks lead onto a bolt-protected slab. A hard traverse left at the fourth bolt gains a crack that runs to a bolted anchor on a stance.
Up a corner, then follow the crack on its right wall to a ledge. Belay on the right end of the ledge.
A short hand crack leaves the corner and meets a crack that traverses right. Climb the four-inch splitter on the face, then more crack to a slanting ledge. Belay at its left end.

Step left and scramble to the next crack, then follow its rightward-trending system to a wide-looking lieback flake and belay there. This pitch and the next can be combined by a leader comfortable on the flake above the stance.
Lieback the flake up and left and work through some roof features. Two bolts protect good face climbing to a large ledge.
Corner systems lead to the top.

review.changed: Wrote all 6 pitches (feet to metres). No rappel table: text only says to rappel the neighbouring route with a single 70 m rope.
review.other_findings: none

pitch_detail.notes: Finger-sized gear in a left-facing corner, then a traverse right to a ramp trending left. A couple of bolts guard some fun liebacking up to the belay.
Keep following the golden corner with good gear and bolts as needed. Where it ends, cross the golden face up and to the right to an anchor.
The golden face continues, then flakes lead to a big ledge. One way to finish from here is on Unknown Upper Brownstone, so the upper pitches may follow that line.
Cracks on the face lead through a roof, then up and left to another stance with an anchor.
Cracks go up and right, then back left to the top.

review.changed: Text labels two pitches 'P4' (5.10c then 5.8); I filed the second as pitch 5 to match the stored count of 5. No rappel table (single 70 m only). The note about Unknown Upper Brownstone is ambiguous in the text; hedged.
review.other_findings: none

pitch_detail.notes: Balance moves reach a large flake you can walk right along. Go up to the first bolt of a neighbouring bolt ladder, downclimb a seam, and make a hard step across to an undercling, the pitch crux. A golden dike then leads to the last ladder bolt; at a big knob step right and climb a corner on the right-facing side past a bolt and small roof to a ledge. This pitch is shared with another route.
Move left onto the dike with a high first bolt. A thin, committing stretch relaxes after two more bolts; the dike at the fourth bolt is tricky, and the last ten metres or so are easy to a stance.

Stay on the dike, which is thinner than below. Whether the third, fourth or fifth bolt is hardest depends on your height. A rest mid-pitch precedes a last crux past three close bolts, then a big traverse left along a good ledge.

Descend a step and traverse right to the dike, to a high first bolt, then left to a corner. Lieback it with gear when possible; it narrows to a hand crack under a roof. Exit left, climb flakes, and at the next roof either go left through a tree or lieback right with less protection.

Chimney past a bolt to flakes on the right, lieback until you can re-wedge in the chimney, and continue up wide terrain to stacked blocks, some hollow. Flared cracks past four bolts reach a poor stance under a roof; a full 60 m rope can link it with the next pitch.
Undercling right across the roof to big jugs, then back left up a crack to a second roof. Jam over it, then easy climbing for about ten metres to a good ledge.

Take the dike on the left of the ledge, four bolts of 5.9, then right to a crack needing gear for about 12 m. Difficulty rises on steepening rock. The free line uses bolts with black hangers on the left: leave the corner at the third, reach a distant jug on the arete, then a power move to a crimp and sustained moves right. Finish around a detached block, back left to a small ledge. Extend the last two bolts to cut drag.

Back around the corner onto a well-featured face, with crack gear available on the right. Difficulty jumps at the first bolt, with several thin technical sections between close bolts. Check nut placements above the last bolt, then traverse left on finger locks to a good ledge.
Finger locks in a corner, with the hard move just above the belay. Past some flakes a tough step left leads out of the corner, then easy bushy cracks to a so-so stance. Short and often dirty.

The free line leaves the original aid crack and face climbs left on large knobs, clipping a high bolt before a hard move onto a golden dike. Past another bolt, climb two ledges, reach a detached block, place gear, and step hard right to a sloping ledge and belay.

Downclimb right to a crack and flake system, place a high piece, then a friction move around the arete. Blocky ground leads to an offwidth up and slightly left, a reachy mantel, and more broken terrain before a rightward traverse to a large leaning block with a splitter on its left side. Step right to a dirty dihedral, fingerlock it past another offwidth and manzanita to a large sandy ledge. Can be split at a gear belay before the traverse.

A wide crack past a few bushes leads to a large ledge, then left into a chimney. Either continue the easier but poorer-rock chimney (about 70 m), or work up the gully to a dirty rightward undercling at 5.10 and a wide flake system to a wedged-block belay (about 60 m).

From the top of the chimney, follow the groove past a large chockstone to bushy ledges, where you can belay or simul-climb. Alternatively, a long 5.7 traverse from the top of the wide flakes reaches the same ledges.
Work up bushy blocks to an easy slab leading up and right beneath a slanting chimney, with an optional belay at its top.
Broken rock trends up and left to a tree belay on the summit, about 150 m above the bushy ledges.

review.changed: Wrote P1-13 individually, P14 and P15 as one linked entry, and the final summit stretch as 16 (stored count 17; text gives 15 numbered plus a final stretch). P11 and P12 lengths from text (70 m; 60-70 m, filed as 65). Lengths in P13 and P14-15 not stated. No rappel table: text gives only which anchors to use, not a station list.
review.other_findings: Text says a rappel from the top of the 10th pitch with a 70 m rope works, using an aid belay at pitch 7 and a midway anchor on pitch 4.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin in a big corner facing left at the lower left of the wall, climb it, and traverse right beneath a large roof. Pass two old bolts and a short shallow corner to reach the foot of a big snow ramp. Belay from two newer bolts on the left.
Kick steps up easy snow for around 75 m, hunting for a hidden corner system on the left whose wall faces right. Belay at its base.
Ice runnels through a left-leaning gully section lead into the upper gully system. Pass a big ice pillar on its left, then a short, hard chimney to a belay stance.
Follow the narrow gully to a vertical chimney ending in a belay cave right under a large chockstone roof.
Chimney up and out to the edge of the chockstone roof and turn it. The gully stays steep and narrow to a second cave beneath another chockstone. Spindrift pouring over the lip is the crux hazard.

Turn one more airy chockstone roof, then easy ground leads to the buttress top. Angle left up the headwall to a corner facing left. An alternative goes straight up, belays at the next cliff band, then climbs a left-facing corner on the right side of a big cleft (M5+, about 46 m).
A short, steep corner and one last chimney lead to easier terrain above.

review.changed: Wrote the 7 numbered pitches; the pitch 6-7 alternative is folded into P6 notes. Left out all rappel info (text only advises rapping the route).
review.other_findings: Stored pitch count 8; text lists 7 plus an alternate and says one or two more pitches may be needed on the headwall.

pitch_detail.notes: A low-angle ice ramp rises for about 45 m to where the wall steepens. Screws hold well. Belay from newly placed bolts on the left wall.
Optional short pitch. Ice face trending left to a small snow ledge. Belay on screws; a two-pin and rock-thread anchor also exists, but carry fresh cord to rebuild it.

A narrowing tube with thinning ice. A new bolt was added in December 2024 and a pin re-hammered to protect the topout. Small cams in the smaller sizes may fit. Past the bulge, an easy snow ramp leads to a new bolted anchor on the wall's right.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches. No rappel table: two rappels described without lengths or anchors per station. No grades for P1 and P3 (text gives none).
review.other_findings: none

pitch_detail.notes: Easy climbing with some loose rock, up the arete's right flank from the ledge. Place little until the headwall to limit drag, since a strong leader can link it with the next pitch on a 70 m rope.
Go left up the chimney. Good protection and engaging moves. Linking with pitch 1 makes a long pitch of about 53 m.
A short jam crack; if linking, skip gear and place high in the crack. An alternative of thin cracks on steeper rock is mentioned, with a harder grade, roughly 5.9+.
Follow the arete along the obvious line of travel. Linkable into one long easy pitch; place gear sparingly to cut drag.

Move the belay and scramble the easy fourth-class ground unroped, about ten metres, to a solid anchor under an alcove. Climb the hands-over-a-roof alcove, then traverse, with one piton, to the wide crack. Pitches 6 to 8 can link to near the top on a 70 m rope.
The standard way goes left, skips the short wide crack, and rejoins a slab on easy arete terrain. The crack (about 5.7) is optional. Continue up easy ground trending slightly left.
A short scramble up easy ground to the summit plateau.

review.changed: Wrote 7 entries covering 8 pitches (4 and 5 treated as one, as the text does). Feet converted to metres.
review.other_findings: none

pitch_detail.notes: A thin finger crack with some layback leads into a splitter hand crack and a stance.
Climb to a roof, then traverse hard to the left beneath it using wide hands and fists. Pop around onto the far side and move up and left to a ledge.
Continue left and a little downward into the next splitter system. Follow a hand and fist crack, with an offwidth move, through two steep roofs to a ledge.
Take the obvious hand crack (about 5.9), or the thin crack to its right (about 5.10+), into a V-slot, then easier ground to boulders at the top.

review.changed: Wrote 4 short pitches; the text is deliberately brief. P4 given the easier grade with the harder variant in notes. No rappel table: descent mentions slings, then two bolted rappels, without a clean station list.
review.other_findings: Gear note: text suggests triples in #3 and two #4s.

pitch_detail.notes: Knifeblade arete climbing. Low down, small cams with runners protect, then clip bolts to the anchor, with the crux right under it.

pitch_detail.anchor: 2 bolts, right side on a small ledge
pitch_detail.notes: Engaging start, then a dihedral-arete section, then a face finish. Bring about 16 quickdraws plus a small cam on a runner for the last piece.
Steep blocky arete with several boulder-problem moves.
Climb left off the anchor into an offwidth section with lots of face relief; small gear protects the wide part. Bring runners and large nuts. A bolted line beside it is a closed project.
Short finish; a few pieces, including mid-size cams, for the summit anchor.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches. No rappel table: text gives only a rope length and rappel count for the standard descent.
review.other_findings: none

pitch_detail.notes: Start on a big ledge below the wide crack on the left. Climb past big blocks to a dihedral, follow its hand crack around the corner, then hands and fists into easy blocky terrain. Anchors can be built almost anywhere.
Pick any of the ledges angling up and left onto the arete, turn the corner, and go straight up to a good ledge. Belay in headwall cracks. Exposed but easy.

Traverse left with small gear to an exposed move onto blocks, up and left to a sharp corner formed by a leaning block, then back right through a series of left-facing corners. Belay on a sloping stance below a harder finger crack in a dihedral.
Climb the dihedral, a thinner finger crack, to the top and belay.

review.changed: Wrote all 4 pitches; text gives no lengths or bolt counts.
review.other_findings: none

pitch_detail.notes: The main event: as a pure ice line it is a steep pillar and curtain, though sun often leaves it aerated or chandeliered. Mixed versions exist, left (more usual) or right of the dihedral. Right side starts in a crack system about six metres right, runout M4 or M5 to a flake traversing left, then very hard moves to reach the hanging ice. Belay atop the pitch with ice screws and some rock gear.
A moderate short pitch to the top of the wall.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches; no per-pitch grades or lengths other than P2 (40 ft). Text is a variation discussion, so P1 notes are thin.
review.other_findings: Stored length_m 43 vs 12 m P2 plus unstated P1.

pitch_detail.notes: Starts as a big, low-angle ice slab and is moderate, leading toward the steeper section. Screws only.

The crux: steeper ice that often forms wide with many options. Generally the further right you go, the easier it gets. Stopping here is possible, traversing right to a bowl and descending, though that slope is prone to slab avalanches.

review.changed: Wrote only P1 and P2, the pitches the text describes. One or two more easy pitches above are mentioned without detail, so not padded.
review.other_findings: Text says commonly 3 pitches, sometimes 4, originally submitted as 5; stored 3 is consistent.

pitch_detail.notes: Easy scrambling from the trail reaches a ramp. Stay on the face while moving left along the bolts, gain the ramp, and do a short V0/V1 sequence up to the belay ledge.
Two early hard moves, then cruising climbing to the next anchor. Back-clean the fourth bolt to limit drag. Can link with the next pitch, skipping bolts and using alpine draws.
Easier climbing to a catwalk ledge; the last six metres or so cross the catwalk to the anchors.
A connecting pitch from another route. The hard move is at the fourth bolt, harder if you are short; stem to clip it.
An easy slab, then interesting face climbing. Links easily with the next pitch.
A dihedral, then stemming through an interesting crux. From here, stay left to finish on this route or take the right-hand bolts to finish on the neighbouring Enrage line.
The left-hand bolts climb a dihedral to a ledge, then tricky face moves follow. Can link with the last pitch using alpine draws.
The last dihedral runs to the top, with two stemming cruxes along the way.

review.changed: Wrote all 8 pitches with bolts and lengths (feet to metres). No rappel table: text gives raps in terms of pitch combinations, not anchors.
review.other_findings: Text: 70 m rope does 7 raps (combine P5 and P6), 60 m rope needs 8.

pitch_detail.notes: Follow the right-hand line up a slab with a hard spot near bolt 7, then trend back left near the top to join the anchor shared with the sister finish.
Clip a few shared bolts, then step right to the arete. The crux is around bolt 11, and this is the line that tops out.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches. Rappel table omitted (refers to the main route).
review.other_findings: Access: first 6 pitches of The Zephyr.

pitch_detail.anchor: screws in the watercourse or trees
pitch_detail.notes: A wide, classic ice pitch. Belay on screws in the watercourse or on trees above, then walk up the slope to the next pitch.
Climb the large bell-shaped flow to a short, stout curtain, then belay from trees above. Best done as a single long pitch.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches. No rappel table: descent says two double-rope rappels from trees, v-threads or boulders without ordered stations.
review.other_findings: Pitch lengths sum to 110 m vs stored 91 m.

pitch_detail.notes: Turn around on the ramp and climb the inconspicuous pillar. Poor rock leads to a roof and V-notch; turn the roof, then spooky flakes to a comfortable ledge.
Bouldery moves into the overhang, protected by a small offset cam, then a rest. Steep fingers and thin technical climbing with tricky gear, wider ground, then steep 5.10 to the anchor.

Low-angle ledgy rock goes up and right to the slab, small gear to its first bolt, then up and right into a finger crack and hands splitter. Hard moves past vegetation reach a roof; climb through and follow a low-angle corner to the anchor up and left.
Straightforward climbing with tricky gear to an arching roof with a single bolt. Bouldery moves go straight up to a ledge, then right to a good ledge under the giant orange dihedral.
A low-angle splitter steepens into big hands in the orange dihedral. Do not follow it to the top; traverse left through large flakes, airy and sparsely protected, to a stance beside the Wild Fang.

A boulder problem through the Wild Fang, then a splitter to the arete and an airy mantel round the corner. Wide flakes to a stance, around another corner to a finger crack under a roof. Pull through to hard laybacking and sporty moves right to the anchor.

Continue up the right-facing dihedral with hard layback moves, thin hands and a small roof into a wide flare, then fists and offwidth. Pass another roof on its right, rest below the black band, and solve a runout rightward move through it to an easy corner and ledge.
A huge dihedral facing left leads to a broad ledge close to the summit plateau.

review.changed: Wrote all 8 pitches with grades, lengths and anchors. No rappel table: descent is a prose set of options, not ordered stations.
review.other_findings: Pitch lengths sum to ~320 m vs stored 335 m; close.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb the first pitch of the neighbouring route but stop below the huge chockstone rather than at its fixed gear.

Find the finger crack to the right and follow it past the chockstone's left, then right through the tunnel to a good stance. A short extra pitch follows to a ledge at the base of the neighbour's third pitch, where you move the belay.

A small crack at the far left of the ledge leads to a dark cave. Pull around its right with good gear, up a wide crack to a solid ledge, and belay in the corner. An alternative pulls the obvious roof crack to a very hard mantle with scarce gear, unrated and guessed somewhere around M8 to M9.
A dihedral, leaving at the end of the corner system on the right, to a ledge at the top.
A short pitch to the end of the technical difficulties. Keep far left; the crack straight ahead is awkward and poorly protected.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches; unnumbered belay-move pitch folded into P2 notes, P3 alternative into P3 notes. P3 left ungraded. No rappel table.
review.other_findings: none

pitch_detail.notes: Begin off the ground on funky terrain below the first roof; get around it and rest. After placing good gear, the vertical terrain has poor feet and technical hooks. An odd bulge with a good pin leads to an alcove belay below the second roof.
Commit to the overhang: good gear but poor feet. After turning the roof, insecure M5+ climbing leads to a ledge. Pitches 1 and 2 could be linked but gear runs short.

Start up left in a corner with a thin crack five feet right. Place a piece, then commit to the M5+ crack, where gear improves with height. Choose your own terrain, with a mantel, to a big ledge on the far left below a wide dihedral crack.

Climb the dihedral about three metres, then traverse right along a small ledge to the base of a seam on a seemingly blank face. Commit to the seam; it ends in an M5+ dihedral to a great ledge. Do not go all the way up the first dihedral; it leads to a slab.
Easy broken terrain to the top.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches; no lengths or anchors stated. Mixed grades as given.
review.other_findings: none
